newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cohen says not insisting military chief be "perfect".
newsitem.headline: Cohen says not insisting military chief be "perfect".

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Thursday he would not insist on "absolute perfection" in his search for a new commander of American military forces.

Cohen spoke just days after Air Force General Joseph Ralston withdrew from consideration as a top candidate to become chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff over an adulterous affair that he, Ralston, had 13 years ago.

"I will look for the best possible individual, but I am not going to insist that there be absolute perfection in every human being that comes up for consideration," the secretary told reporters who travelled to Brussels with him for a NATO meeting.

Cohen, who is expected to recommend an officer in the coming weeks to President Bill Clinton to succeed Army General John Shalikashvili on September 30, said in an interview that he did not regret supporting Ralston despite the decade-old affair.

"Everybody is human and they may have different frailties," said the secretary, promising that "a very high standard will be exacted" in his continuing search among senior generals and admirals to fill the nation's top military job.

News of Ralston's affair, which occurred while he was separated from his first wife, sparked charges by Congress that senior officers and men were not being treated as severely over sexual misdemeanours as junior officers and women in the U.S. military.
The Senate must confirm Shalikashvili's successor. Ralston withdrew to avoid a heated, public fight over his nomination by Clinton for the job.
"He thought, and I believed, that he could have ultimately won confirmation," Cohen told reporters.

The secretary denied there was any intentional unfairness in the military justice system despite controversial public pressure by the Air Force last month that forced its first woman bomber pilot, Lt. Kelly Flinn, to resign to avoid a court martial on adultery and other charges.

"I would like to search for perfection. If I could find it, I would certainly nominate that individual ... but I don't want to raise any expectations that anyone who has a flaw in his character, whatever that might be, will be an automatic disqualification."

Defence officials said privately that, while Cohen was not yet near a final decision, candidates under consideration included Army General Wesley Clark. He has already been nominated by Clinton to become Supreme Allied Commander of NATO forces in Europe.
Also being considered, they said, were the commanders of the different U.S. military branches and chiefs of American military commands around the world.
